question_text: An ML engineer is deciding between one-hot encoding and label encoding for a categorical feature representing customer regions such as North America, Europe, and Asia Pacific. The feature has no natural ordering. The model being trained is a logistic regression. Which encoding technique should be used and why?
explanation: One-hot encoding is correct for nominal categorical features with no natural ordering when using linear models. Label encoding assigns arbitrary integers (e.g. 0,1,2) which implies a false ordinal relationship that linear models will exploit incorrectly — the model would interpret Asia Pacific as mathematically twice Europe. One-hot encoding creates separate binary columns per category eliminating this false relationship.
option_text: Label encoding, because logistic regression requires integer inputs

question_text: A dataset contains a feature representing annual customer income with values ranging from $10,000 to $10,000,000. The distribution is heavily right-skewed with most customers earning under $100,000 and a small number of high-value outliers. A linear regression model is being trained. Which transformation should the ML engineer apply to this feature?
explanation: Log transformation reduces right skewness by compressing the range of large values and expanding small ones. This stabilizes variance and helps linear models that assume normally distributed features. Normalization and standardization scale the data but do not fix the underlying skewness. Binning loses information and is not the right choice for a regression target feature.
option_text: Apply min-max normalization to scale the feature to the range 0 to 1

question_text: A company runs a K-Nearest Neighbors model to classify customer support tickets. The feature set includes numeric fields such as response time in seconds, ticket priority score from 1 to 5, and days since last contact ranging from 0 to 365. Log transformation addresses skewness not range differences. One-hot encoding is for categorical features.
